setupSteps: Check the machine is empty or loaded evenly. Plates on the sled's weight horns (pegs) must be equal on both sides. Unload anything left by the last person if it is too heavy for you (and return plates to the rack).

Find the safety catches before loading. Most sleds have two handles beside the seat that rotate the catches in (locked) or out (free). Some also have adjustable safety stops (bars or pins) that stop the sled from coming down past a set point. Ask staff to show you how this specific model works; designs vary.
Set the safety stops (if the machine has them) at a point just below your planned lowest position, so the sled cannot crush you if you fail a rep (est.; follow the machine's labels).

Set the backrest angle (if adjustable). A more upright back gives less depth; a more reclined back gives more. ExRx: set the back support so you get near-full range without your hips rounding off the pad. Beginners: middle setting (est.).

First set: start with the empty sled. The sled itself has weight (it varies by model; check the machine label or ask staff; Indian model sled weights Not found). Because the sled runs at 45°, the force you push is roughly 70% (sin 45° ≈ 0.71) of the sled-plus-plate weight, slightly less because of rail friction (geometry estimate; secondary sources only, est.). Do not compare your number with a friend's on a different machine.

Load plates (later sets): largest plates first, close to the frame, equal on both sides; add collars/clips if the horns have them. Load and unload one side at a time only if the sled is locked on its catches.
Sit: back and tailbone flat against the backrest, head resting on the headrest.
Foot plate position: feet in the middle of the plate, hip-width apart (NASM), toes pointing forward or turned out a little (5–15°, est.). Whole foot on the plate, heels down.

Foot height: middle of the plate is the default. Higher on the plate works the buttocks a bit more; lower works the front thighs more (ExRx; one small EMG study in 14 women found higher gluteus maximus activity with feet high and higher quadriceps activity with feet low). Too low lifts the heels and stresses the knees.
Hands: hold the side handles (not the knees).
Unrack: push the sled up until your legs are straight but not locked, then turn the safety handles outward to free the sled. Keep the hands on the handles.
Pin: put the selector pin fully into the lightest or second-lightest plate of the stack (Gym 4). Push it all the way in.
Seat/back pad: move the seat (usually a lever or pop-pin, often numbered) so that with your feet on the plate your knees bend to about 90° (ACE; NASM). Note the number for next time.
Sit: back and tailbone against the backrest (ACE), head relaxed.
Feet: hip-width, toes forward or slightly out, heels flat, middle of the plate (ACE: toes forward, heels flat).
Hands: lightly hold the handles (ACE) and brace the stomach.
Range limiter (if fitted): set it so the stack cannot go deeper than your comfortable depth.

steps.part: A. 45° sled leg press (main steps; the seated machine is the same from step 2 on, without catches)
steps.title: Brace
steps.action: With the sled unlocked and legs straight but soft (not locked), gently tighten your stomach as if about to cough.
steps.feel: Lower back and buttocks pressed into the pad.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back and hips flat on the pad, knees slightly bent. Front: knees in line with feet.

steps.part: A. 45° sled leg press (main steps; the seated machine is the same from step 2 on, without catches)
steps.title: Lower the sled
steps.action: Bend your knees and hips together to let the sled come slowly toward you.
steps.feel: Thighs and buttocks working to control the weight; a stretch in the buttocks near the bottom.
steps.breathing: Keep breathing in, or hold a light brace, as you lower.
steps.visualCheck: Side: knees bend toward the shoulders, heels stay on the plate. Front: knees point the same way as the toes (NASM: knees in line with the middle toes), not caving in.

steps.part: A. 45° sled leg press (main steps; the seated machine is the same from step 2 on, without catches)
steps.title: Stop at your depth
steps.action: Stop when your knees are bent to about 90° (beginner default; NASM returns to about 90°), or earlier if your hips start to roll up off the pad (ExRx; Muscle & Strength: stop just before the lower back comes off the pad).
steps.feel: Strong thigh tension, no pinch in the lower back or kneecap.
steps.visualCheck: Side: knees about 90° bent; tailbone still on the seat. Front: knees over the second toe.

steps.part: A. 45° sled leg press (main steps; the seated machine is the same from step 2 on, without catches)
steps.title: Press
steps.action: Push through the whole foot (heel and mid-foot) to straighten the legs and drive the sled away.
steps.feel: Front thighs and buttocks doing the work; heels heavy.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as you push (never hold the breath through the whole rep).
steps.visualCheck: Side: heels stay down, hips stay on the pad. Front: knees track over the toes, do not snap inward.

steps.part: A. 45° sled leg press (main steps; the seated machine is the same from step 2 on, without catches)
steps.title: Stop just short of lockout
steps.action: Stop with the knees almost straight but still soft (Livestrong-quoted trainer: about 10° short of fully straight; NASM: don't lock out).
steps.feel: Weight held by the muscles, not the joint.
steps.breathing: Finish breathing out, then breathe in.
steps.visualCheck: Side: a small bend still visible at the knee.

steps.part: A. 45° sled leg press (main steps; the seated machine is the same from step 2 on, without catches)
steps.title: Repeat for the planned reps

steps.part: A. 45° sled leg press (main steps; the seated machine is the same from step 2 on, without catches)
steps.title: Rack the sled (45° only)
steps.action: At the top of the last rep, turn the safety handles back in so the catches are engaged, then let the sled rest on them gently.
steps.feel: Sled held by the catches before you relax the legs.
steps.visualCheck: Catches clearly locked before you take your feet off the plate.

steps.part: A. 45° sled leg press (main steps; the seated machine is the same from step 2 on, without catches)
steps.title: Seated machine finish: return the stack slowly until the plates touch silently; then lift your feet off

commonMistakes.title: Going too deep so the hips lift and the lower back rounds
commonMistakes.text: Going too deep so the hips lift and the lower back rounds. Why: the pelvis tucks under and the lower back bends under load, which may increase shear forces on the lumbar spine (clinical trial protocol note; efdeportes article). Fix: set the backrest/safety stops so you stop just before the tailbone leaves the seat; beginner depth about 90° at the knee.

commonMistakes.title: Locking the knees at the top
commonMistakes.text: Locking the knees at the top. Why: lockout puts the load on the joint; a JBJS case report describes a lifter who dislocated both knees after locking out under very heavy load (one case, but it supports caution). Fix: stop about 10° short of straight.

commonMistakes.title: Knees caving in on the press
commonMistakes.text: Knees caving in on the press. Why: strains the inside of the knee and wastes force. Fix: lighter load, knees over the second toe (NASM; Physitrack: push the knees outward).

commonMistakes.title: Heels lifting off the plate
commonMistakes.text: Heels lifting off the plate. Why: the knees travel forward and kneecap stress rises; the push shifts to the toes. Fix: move the feet a little higher and push through the heels (ExRx).

commonMistakes.title: Bouncing at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Bouncing at the bottom. Why: momentum and a sudden load on the knees and back (NASM lists bouncing as a common error). Fix: 2–3 seconds down, a short pause, then press.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath and straining on every rep
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath and straining on every rep. Why: leg press produced the highest blood pressures of all lifts studied by MacDougall et al. (1985): group mean peak 320/250 mmHg in experienced bodybuilders lifting to failure, partly from the Valsalva (breath-hold) effect. Fix: breathe out on the press, stop 2–3 reps before failure.

commonMistakes.title: Loading too much and doing tiny half-reps (ego loading)
commonMistakes.text: Loading too much and doing tiny half-reps (ego loading). Why: big numbers, little work, higher joint stress. Fix: choose a load that allows full planned depth for all reps (Gym 4 finder sets).

commonMistakes.title: Forgetting the safety catches / unloading one side
commonMistakes.text: Forgetting the safety catches / unloading one side. Why: an unlocked sled can drop; uneven plates can twist the sled. Fix: always lock the catches before getting out; unload evenly.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing on the knees with the hands
commonMistakes.text: Pushing on the knees with the hands. Why: takes work off the legs and can push knees inward. Fix: hands on the handles.

safetyNotes: Knee problems: use the short-range version (45–60° of knee bend) and a light load; stop if kneecap pain increases.
Lower back problems: go only as deep as your tailbone stays on the seat; the seated machine may feel easier; stop with leg pain or numbness.

High blood pressure / heart disease: breathe out on every press, avoid sets to failure and heavy singles (MacDougall 1985: leg press gave the highest blood pressures measured). Do not lift if resting BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher; get clearance at 140–179/90–119 (secondary ACSM-aligned sources).

Pregnancy: choose the seated or 45° machine over any flat-lying version, reduce load, widen the feet and limit depth so the belly is not squashed, no breath-holding; ask your obstetrician (ACOG supports continued strength training for healthy pregnancies; leg-press-specific advice comes from secondary sources).
Hip replacement or recent knee/hip surgery: deep hip bending may be restricted; follow your surgeon's limits.
Larger bodies: check the machine's maximum user weight (e.g., some commercial seated models list 136 kg or 150 kg).
